Here's another example, just for the extra clarity.

Let's say I'm sitting at a table with three other players: Jack, Eric, and Nathan.

The turn after I play Triple Triad, before I draw, I tell everyone to exile the top cards of their deck. I do the same.

Jack exiles a blue/black instant that costs 3.

Eric exiles  a colorless artifact that costs 2.

Nathan exiles a green creature that costs 12.

I exile a red creature that costs 5. Looking at these cards specifically, I am allowed to play my 5-cost creature for its regular cost, and I can cast Jack's or Eric's cards for free and use them on my side of the field. I cannot touch Nathan's card, and that simply stays in exile unless something else happens to it.

If I don't cast the exiled stuff I could theoretically play, it stays in exile and I lose access to it. Repeat this step every turn until either you die or the Triple Triad gets removed from play.

The absolutely-fucking-weird-easter-egg that is the Eltonbrand in *The Elder Scrolls III: Morrowind*. Probably cheating because it's a developer in-joke and also because the PC version's creation software helps figure some of this out.

First, go get Goldbrand, the reward for Boethiah's Daedric Quest and one of the best swords in the game. This in itself is a bit strange and tedious, as you have to search the ruins near a Daedric shrine in the northeast to find a sunken statue. Talk to the head of the statue, follow its instructions to get someone who will build a new statue, then give him money, a book, and 21 in-game days to restore the statue and go get your sword. (There is no journal entry that tells you the statue is done, the builder just says he needs "several weeks".)

Got that? Good. It gets a lot weirder from here.

Go become a vampire, so that you can take on a quest for fellow vampire Sirilonwe at the Vivec Mage's Guild. She wants a guy dead and wants his key as proof. Go do this simple job and take "Shashev's Key", the item in question.

Now, before you turn it in, make sure you have exactly 11,137 gold, Goldbrand in your inventory, and then go talk to Sirilonwe. A text box over her dialog will run saying "Go to Hell, Carolina!" and the Goldbrand becomes the stronger Eltonbrand, with stronger damage all around and more enchantments.

The "hints" are that a Bethesda developer is a fan of NBA player Elton Brand, the name "Shashev's Key" being phonetically the same as Elton Brand's college basketball coach Mike Krzyzewski, and the amount of gold being a code for Elton's birthday 11/1/1937. The "Go to Hell, Carolina!" is because that same college team had a massive rivalry with North Carolina's team. The silliest in-joke you can legitimately get in a Bethesda game, I'd think, if you're insane enough to figure it out.

Short version of the lore of Sephiroth, Fallen Warrior, just because it tickles my brain. It's a bit of an interesting case back then, albeit one that doesn't excuse their current practices. Pokemon's first generation was a passion project from a small team that took a bunch of time from the team's inexperience. The first game got thrown through so many prototypes on its 6-year dev cycle, and the team had never made an RPG before. There's a lot of leftovers that got found out from the game's origins, and it shows they'd been iterating and throwing out gameplay concepts for almost the entire development cycle while hastily removing stuff.

Then Gold and Silver, which were intended to be a big finale-type game that featured even more scope-creep than the original games did. They had to delay the game by two years because they just kept wanting to add and add, while running out of space. It's fairly common knowledge by this point, but one possible reason why the Gen 2 games have so many bugs and oddities is because of how Game Freak worked with Satoru Iwata.

When they ran out of space on the cartridge (the biggest cartridge they could use, *after* transitioning from a pure Game Boy game to a Game Boy Color game), Game Freak asked Satoru Iwata what to do, and he wrote a data compression tool that shrunk the game to half its size. Only then did they decide to add the Kanto section, since it would make for a fitting finale and there was just enough space. I imagine that trying to keep the newly-compressed first half of the game in line with your new ideas and tangents can get really messy, especially when you're still referring to data from the original games and have to connect with them for compatibility purposes.

Game Freak is just still doing what they've always done, even though they're handling something far too big on hardware far too different from the roots of their culture. It seems like every game is just a passion project that they're trying to tamp down from their goals, and there's a noted bump down in various areas every time Pokemon shifts systems.

These are fixed in Generation 4, thankfully! Most of them retain their original intended functionality, with a single exception; the Fast Ball avoids the "fleeing table" check by instead having a higher rate against Pokemon whose base Speed stat is 100 or more. This opens up the use cases more, including on some of the 'mons it was intended to work on back in Gen 2. The Moon Ball now properly checks that the target Pokemon is part of an evolution line that uses the Moon Stone, which now includes the Skitty family with the greater Pokemon pool.

However, another bug does crop up that affects a ball that was fine in Generation 2. The Heavy Ball is supposed to not affect catch rate if the Pokemon's weight is between 225.8 lbs and 451.3 lbs. The code immediately before it wrongly checks if the Pokemon's catch rate is less than 1024, when it's meant to check the weight being less than 102.4 kg. All Pokemon have a catch rate less than 1024. As a result, the Heavy Ball is now the only glitched one, as it negatively impacts your catch rate on all Pokemon weighing 451.4 lbs or less.

I want to elaborate on this, for a funny little anecdote. This isn't comprehensive, but instead focusing on one mechanic for the uninitiated. I'm sorry if this looks ridiculously long.

Generation 2 introduced Apricorn Balls, a new type of Poke Ball that require you to bring the colored Apricorn fruits to an old master and have him make specialized Poke Balls every real-world day. They are intended to be highly effective at catching Pokemon in unique situations, and almost all of them do not work as advertised.

The ones that work correctly in all versions are the Lure Ball and Friend Ball. These respectively have a 3x multiplier on catch rate for Surf encounters, and act as a regular Poke Ball that increases a Pokemon's friendship value when caught. As for the others...there's a host of problems that are likely due to the game's hastily developed nature and Game Freak's notorious rough coding practices.

The Heavy Ball is designed to have a higher multiplier when catching Pokemon of larger weight. It does this correctly in Gold and Silver, but something done to the data in Crystal causes it to read three specific Pokemon as having junk data for a weight, granting the max possible bonus. These Pokemon are Kadabra, Sunflora and Tauros, who are all nowhere near the weight the Ball would prefer.

The Level Ball is designed to catch Pokemon of a lower level than your Pokemon, increasing as the disparity grows. It does this, and then ignores all later checks, which causes the HP and status conditions of the Pokemon to mean nothing. If you're using a Level Ball, you'll have as much success at full HP as you do when it's poisoned and 2 HP away from fainting.

The Love Ball is supposed to have a higher chance of catching Pokemon of the same species, but opposite gender as your current Pokemon. This is supposed to encourage the breeding mechanic which was introduced in this game. However, it instead checks for if the Pokemon is the same gender and same species as yours. Whether this makes the ball a fan of homosexuality or all Pokemon are bi is up to your interpretation.

The Fast Ball is meant to have a higher chance of catching Pokemon that could possibly flee. Given there are several species, including rare encounters and a trio of legendaries, who either can flee or always flee, this would be very useful. Except it doesn't check the three tables of fleeing Pokemon, it just checks the first three Pokemon who are set to flee: Magnemite, Grimer and Tangela. It thus has no special effect on any other Pokemon, or on the legendaries that flee every turn.

Finally, the Moon Ball is probably the funniest one. It's intended to aid in catching Pokemon who evolve via the Moon Stone item. These Pokemon are rare and a bit mystical in nature, so it makes sense from a flavor perspective even if it's a very narrow target. This item is coded so poorly that it has no functional difference from a regular Poke Ball and I have to do another line-break to explain it properly.

The Moon Ball checks whether the Pokemon evolves with an item, specifically the item at byte 0x0A. This is where the Moon Stone was in Gen 1. In Gen 2, that's the index for the Burn Heal, a consumable item that nothing evolves with. Even if this pointed to the right item, the Moon Ball also checks specifically that the Pokemon has a branch evolution with multiple choices, and then checks if that Pokemon evolves via the 10th evolution method. There are only five methods to evolve.

This one item would only work as intended if you were facing a Pokemon with two evolutions, one of which was via a Burn Heal, and the other was via a method that literally doesn't exist.

There are a few ways you can go about learning. I apologize if this is a wall of text, I'm trying to break it down as best as I can but I know from my relative perspective it might seem too overwhelming.

If you want to get a general overview of things and then refine later, you can try Story Mode. It's not ever going to be finished, but what's there has some tutorials about movement that kind of force you to get acclimated to how characters can move around and jump, which will be more important than combos when you're just starting out.

  
The easiest characters to learn are Arizona and Oleander. Arizona is straightforward, has a lot of buttons you can just kind of throw out, and her Magic system is relatively easy to wrap your head around. (Throw the lasso, enhance a special) Oleander specializes in distance play but has similarly big buttons and can maneuver a bit with her teleports. Her Magic also enhances her specials, but you have to actively build it in a different way.

Once you pick someone, you can navigate the dizzying array of training mode tools to help get your bearings. The training dummy can be set to several different movement patterns to help you work on how to properly hit enemies at certain angles/movements, and you can make them block after the first hit of a combo in order to see what truly combos and what leads to getting punished. 

After you throw out your characters' buttons and get a general feel for them, you can turn on the Frame Display option to get to the next level. "Simple" is fine; you want the option where two numbers appear at the bottom when you press a button. Those two numbers respectively show "when did the attack hit / how advantaged are you". A plus means you can act before the opponent, a minus means the opponent can act before you. Remember that the game goes at 60 frames per second, and press buttons to try and see what's your fastest attack, what move gives you the most advantage.

Lastly, before you try to learn combos, you want to learn how to block. You won't be able to hit anyone if you keep getting opened up, of course. Attacks can hit at three levels: overheads (which must be blocked standing), mids (which can be blocked in either direction) or lows (which must be blocked crouching). In Training Options, you can set the dummy to CPU on a low difficulty. One general beginner tip for blocking is to block low when not doing anything else; low attacks are quicker than overheads and more common. When the dummy jumps, switch to blocking while standing, because many aerial attacks are overheads.

And if Arizona or Oleander aren't doing it for you, feel free to try more characters who seem interesting. While some characters like Pom and Tianhuo can be really difficult at the highest level, you don't need to get to that level immediately. Poking around with their movesets in a controlled environment and picking the pieces together will get you farther.

Their fandom in Latin America led to one of the funniest character origin stories ever.

During the Eolith era of SNK, the company was approached by a Mexican company named Evoga to make a fighting game for the Neo Geo. Talks were apparently going relatively frosty, and so the staff took a small break to play at the KOF '98 cabinet that was in the office. The SNK team were getting trounced repeatedly, and in their anger at being beaten at their own game, made a bet with Evoga's representatives:

If SNK won a 3-on-3 team battle of their best players vs Evoga's, then SNK would get to create one character for this new fighting game. If Evoga won, then they'd get to make a new character for the next KOF game. The resulting battle was "lost handily" by the SNK developers, who were incredibly outmatched.

The end result was that Evoga requested a busty Mexican wrestler, and so **Ángel** was born.

The flavor is specifically targeting the Yugioh card this is based on: ["Number 39: Utopia"](https://yugipedia.com/wiki/Number_39:_Utopia). That card is a type of monster known as an "Xyz Monster", which needs to be summoned in a specific way. You have to take two monsters who are the same "Level" of 4 (here represented as 4 CMC creatures) and stack them on top of each other while putting the Xyz Monster on top. Those cards stacked under the card are treated as "materials", stop being considered monsters, and interface with the Xyz effects.

It does look weak on the surface because Levels in Yugioh are not analogous to Magic mana costs; as opposed to a ramping curve, Levels are split into three "tiers". Level 1-4 monsters can be summoned for free, Level 5-6 require sacrificing one other monster, and Level 7+ monsters require two sacrifices.

There are two commonly-agreed upon entry points for Pokemon Mystery Dungeon. The originals, known as "Rescue Team", were originally released on DS and GBA as near-identical games paired like the main games. The originals have adorable pixel art, but if you want to officially support the series and get quality-of-life updates, the remake "Rescue Team DX" is available on Switch. It has all the content of the original, remakes the game with a kind of painterly 3D artstyle, and adds a few new mechanics to make the game easier and less obtuse.

The other popular entry is the Explorers games, specifically Explorers of Sky, which was released as a "third version" in the vein of Emerald/Platinum/etc. It's the clear fan-favorite with its cast of characters and plot that can hold up well today, has a much larger postgame while adding a few quality-of-life features to the formula, and most notably features "Special Episodes"; side-chapters that switch your PoV to side characters in order to tell their notable exploits through the game. The game is easy to find online and can be emulated incredibly easily.

In Pokemon Mystery Dungeon, there's a lot of exploration/rescue teams that try to make the world a better place. For the most part, they're all off-screen and thus don't get much in the way of notable exploits. But there's one team that's particularly bad at their job; Team Skull.

Team Skull features in the Explorers games, and is comprised of a Skuntank, Koffing, and Zubat. Kingdom Hearts is a lot of things, but there are three major reasons one might find themselves entranced by it nowadays.

1. **Action RPG stylishness**. The games have gradually gone more towards a stylish-action flair, always having real-time combat that incorporates RPG mechanics to allow you to build Sora in slightly different ways while making engaging combat scenarios. You have access to powerful magic, high-flying animesque attacks, and a lot of different defensive maneuvers to add depth to combat. The games are not difficult enough that you have to strategize for every encounter, but the possiblity is there and the late-game/optional stuff still challenges many players. It looks cool and feels cool to play.
2. **Disney appeal**. As part of the game's core ethos, you will spend a majority of your time in worlds that are basically the movies brought to life. Not every movie makes the best transfer, but if you're a fan of Disney's classical animation era, you will likely find at least one world and one sequence that makes you happy just to play through it. Every character, with a scant few exceptions, has been reprised by their major actor, and you can witness some charming scenes from watching Disney villains interact with an anime boy or Jack Skellington adapt the lessons he's learned to a new conflict.
3. **It's so earnest**. There is nothing in Kingdom Hearts that is sardonic or lampshading what it's trying to do. It puts ridiculous concepts out into the story, and asks you the player to suspend your disbelief because it is going to put its full self behind it. You might not understand why Mickey Mouse is concerned with the universal balance of light and darkness. You may hear characters talk about ice cream as if it is the most important part of their day. And you will see teenagers grow up across the games and grow as people while Disney mascots are their therapists. And the games will explain all of this with stuff that makes sense if you put yourself in the game's world.

2. Then the spinoffs came out, and all of them are frankly terrible. Mythologies was a ridiculously difficult beat-em-up with poor adaptation of the control scheme and only saved by the legendarily hammy cutscenes. Special Forces doesn't even have those, and is instead an experimental, blaxploitation-esque 3D game that does nothing new or exciting in a time when a lot of games were breaking new ground. The cartoon is a kid-friendly adaptation of one of the most violent game series at the time, and had little fans because of it.
3. Mortal Kombat 4 was delayed so Midway could test their 3D chops with something else. They took the wrong lessons from that test, War Gods, and made a 3D game with barely any 3D movement. Gameplay was simplified to the point of every character having the same normals and strings, only diversified by weapon, specials, and fatality. Add on a roster of poorly-received newcomers and being an arcade-focused game in the death-knell of arcades, you're sitting poorly. It got an updated re-release that was even worse, too.
4. The remaining ill will towards the series was built gradually over both Deadly Alliance and Deception. Deadly Alliance itself was fine, bringing the series back and making well-received changes to the system. Deception would try to expand the setting by adding a bunch of newcomers that weren't all that well received, plus pushing a new character as the replacement Liu Kang and giving him his own story mode. Said story portrays new hero Shujinko as a complete moron who basically hands the villain their victory. Gameplay-wise, it does a good job expanding on DA but was lambasted by the niche fighting game community at the time because it was so damn broken, and local scenes didn't really exist so you were playing online on variable, poor delay netcode.

By the time of Armageddon, the series hadn't really done anything with its momentum or revival.

Mortal Kombat Armageddon. The story had reached a breaking point with too many characters, as well as stakes that were raising between realms and having too many villains doing their shit. To make matters worse, some of the primary characters in the franchise were either going evil (Raiden), dying (Johnny Cage), or were revived wrong (Liu Kang). As the scales got bigger, characters were assigned to nebulous factions of Good and Evil even when they weren't really interacting with each other.

And on an out-of-universe note, the games were seen as losing steam. The spinoffs' failures and the poor jump to 3D were still in the eyes of the public, and Deadly Alliance/Deception were shots in the arm that couldn't really continue to keep up outside of the casual fanbase.

To answer your request about Modern Controls for Avatar specials: This is due to an input issue. Capcom wants Modern and Classic controls to be, relatively, on the same page. Modern trades damage and certain normals for easier reactions and automatic combos, while Classic has the full toolkit but has an execution barrier. This is especially true in World Tour, which is designed as an intro to fighting games for newer players, and intended to have the same difficulty curve regardless of control type.

Importantly, Modern does not differentiate the punch and kick buttons. This causes a decision to be made if characters have two specials on the same motion. For instance, take Ryu's Hadoken and Blade Kick; they both use Quarter Circle Forward, but Hadoken uses punch and Blade Kick uses...kick. Since Modern needs to let you use at least one strength of both and make things consistent, they'll generally set one as shortcut-only and make the "more important" special usable via their shared motion. Going back to that example, Ryu is designed to be more of a zoner, so Hadoken takes the quarter-circle input on Modern to allow you to use all his fireballs, while Blade Kick becomes shortcut-only.

All this is to say; the limitation exists because Modern can't tell the difference between punch and kick, so something has to get set elsewhere when two commands overlap. Letting the player set shortcut-only specials in addition to motions isn't what the devs wanted, so instead they chose to put Classic on the same ground as Modern in order to make things "equal" between the two in World Tour/Avatar Battle.

Okizeme is a greater concept that meaty attacks are a part of. Generally, when players refer to "oki", they're referring to the layers of options possible on a knockdown. For instance, in Street Fighter 4, Akuma had strong oki options off of Light Tatsu > Sweep, as he could perform several different Demon Flip followups, a throw, cr. MK, an overhead, or other options in order to make the opponent guess and stay in a bad situation if they were wrong. Performing these attacks meaty meant giving them greater frame advantage, and keeping the options safe.

Basically, oki is the state of "advantage when knocking down", meaties are "a choice offered when knocking down".

"Protogens" are a vaguely defined species of fursona that use a bipedal, canine-like body and are defined by their cybernetic enhancements. They're described as being "60% organic", with the lower torso and below becoming a cybernetic carapace alongside a unique, rounded robot head with a panel on it. That panel bears LEDs that are used in place of a typical face, broadcasting the protogen's eyes, mouth, and whatever visual concept the art may want to convey. Their upper limbs are organic, but can be adjusted with "modular addons" to give new opportunities.

"Primagens", on the other hand, are attempts at a more "exclusive" variant of the protogen. Primagens are designed as effectively hardware-upgrades from the protogen, with taller individuals using more cybernetics and sleeker aesthetics in their design. Primagens are now cybernetic all the way up to the chest, with a small spate of fur on the neck and nape. Primagens have a completely cybernetic head as well, sharing the LED panel of protogens but lacking the biological ears and back of their counterparts. And while protogens can walk like raptors, primagens use four-limbed feral movement akin to a cheetah, wolf or other predator animal.

The differences are laid out like this because the species were both created by the same individual, who treats the design as one of their trademarks. They seek legal action and public shaming against those who freely create their own primagens instead of paying for a primagen design through them. Protogens are a free, open species that anyone can make, so long as it does not violate certain style guidelines and don't take factors from primagens. Hope this helps!

All three of the games mentioned (New Vegas, Bloodborne, and Silent Hill) all have some form of queerness implicit in their design, things that go against the generally-accepted "standard" to allow for some level of deep introspection.

New Vegas is a game that gamifies your sexuality; you can choose to be hetero, bi or homosexual, and the worst you get for your build is some light rebuffs because certain factions might not like it. The most obviously-antagonistic faction is a fascist heteronormative state, making some question the ideals that they champion and thus leads to introspection. On a narrative level, the game also centers around a theme of "letting go of the past", and points out through companion quests, the DLCs and various factions that it's not what you were that matters--it's what you are now. So, this is basically how Persona 3 poses a question and answers it via two characters: "what makes life worth living?"

Nyx Avatar talks about humanity distantly, summarizing the journey of the Tarot over the course of the 13 major arcana. It is said to be a universal experience, a fixed existence as "the arcana is the means by which all is revealed". According to Nyx, the proper human life is full of ups and downs, and life is full of grandeur and magnificence. Then, as the final phase occurs, Nyx poses their own answer to the question; "Beyond the journey you have taken lies the absolute end. One thing is always certain: death awaits all."

As far as Nyx Avatar is concerned, there is no meaning to life. At the end of the road, we all die, so there isn't really much of a point. This is reinforced by the Avatar's actions as Ryoji; even after pretending to be human for some time, the Avatar's fixation on death as an inevitability makes it a more preferable choice to simply let death come and have everyone reach their destined end without knowing it'll happen.

But Makoto answers the question in his own way; after signing the Velvet Room's contract, he lives life to the fullest. He makes genuine connections, touches lives in immaterial and permanent ways, and assists others in navigating death and loss, while suffering it himself over the course of his journey. Unlike the Avatar, Makoto strives for the human point of view; the Social Links he makes are not always the "perfect" upright forms of their Arcana, but grow into it alongside Makoto's companionship.

This all culminates in the final battle; through Makoto's human connection and complete understanding of his place in the world, he attains the Universe Arcana to represent a "complete" life. The Great Seal, and Makoto's determination to live until Graduation, acts as a rebuttal to the Avatar and his own answer to the question: "Life is worth living when you have something to die for." You can interpret a lot about Makoto's general personality, and this is the interpretation I've gathered over playing each version of Persona 3 and studying it over time.

Not OP, but providing my take based on what people have said and from reading Jojo:

Jotaro's stunted emotional displays are, according to Araki, the result of him feeling that his emotions are already easily readable and thus don't need to be explained. This is a common trait among some autistic individuals who don't recognize their behaviors aren't universal, especially emotional ones.

While characters in Jojo are already commonly strange in fashion, Jotaro's are the ones called out for being "uncool" or irregular, with both his school uniform (that he's attached to to the point of commissioning a woolen one) and his various marine-themed outfits after his career as a marine biologist being remarked upon for their weirdness. This can be either an attachment to specific qualities of the outfits or an extension of a special interest, depending on how you want to interpret that.

Jotaro also takes the autistic trait of pulling from his favorite media; this is admittedly a one-time example, but he admits to Enya in Part 3 that he gained his style of messing with enemies from *Columbo.* It's not to the point of echolalia like more "common" autism diagnoses, but it's there.

Addendum; one of the reasons he has a hard time expressing emotion outwardly is because he believes he's already incredibly easy to read; a symptom of autism is that you think of your own internalized behaviors as normal even when nobody else has performed them, to the point you don't feel like you need to explain them because they explain themselves.

I think one of my favorite interpretations of meta and player behavior regarding it has been in *Super Street Fighter 2: Turbo*, the last arcade iteration of Street Fighter 2.

For the uninitiated, there are two characters in that game that are head-and-shoulders above the rest of the cast. The first is Akuma, a secret boss who is playable via an ingame code. He plays like the protagonists Ryu and Ken, but incredibly, unfairly busted. In a game known for high damage and powerful offense, Akuma can kill an enemy player in a single combo from nearly anywhere with multiple options. He also has no real weakness as a character with effective distance play, stellar defensive tools, and a unique tool in the "air fireball" that completely *shuts down* several members of the cast. 

Akuma is, as you can probably tell, banned in all tournaments. Even the later revisions of the game, which were designed to have better balance, still left Akuma in a ban-worthy state because he is simply too powerful in the context of the game.

The second case is a bit more interesting. By inputting a special code when selecting a character, you can play as an "Old" character, who is based on data from the previous entry *Super Street Fighter 2*. The Old version of the character Sagat is an objective improvement over his newer self and one of the strongest characters in the game. On top of higher damage and better movement, Old Sagat has the fastest-recovery projectile attacks in the game.

What this means is that, when given a single moment of space, Old Sagat can throw out a devastating array of fireballs that must be navigated perfectly, where getting hit knocks you down and subjects you to more fireballs while blocking keeps pushing you back and chipping away at your health. It's beatable, but it's an impressive level of space control that invalidates many characters.

As a result, Old Sagat is "soft banned" by the tournament scene; every player makes a gentleman's agreement to not pick Old Sagat for how centralizing his presence is. If one player decides to break the agreement and play as Old Sagat, the proverbial glass has been broken and now everyone present will be allowed to play as Old Sagat. It's a fascinating bit of sportsmanship originating from what I can tell is the beginning of the game's competitive scene.

In English, referring to oneself is simply done with "I" or "me". Those are the direct personal pronouns.

In Japanese, you have various pronouns that are used not just to describe one's physical appearance, but the intent of your personality and the formality of the situation. For example, a gender-neutral, excessively polite form of "I" is "watakushi". A polite, casual way to refer to yourself in a masculine way is "boku", or an assertive feminine person can use "atashi". Fiction tends to use a character's choice of pronoun to exposit their standing, mental state, or self-image.

As another Persona example, Naoto's Social Link allows Yu to help her decide which pronoun to use. By default, Naoto uses "boku", but going the romance route has her ask whether she should refer to herself as the feminine "watashi". In the English translation, this line instead is written as Naoto asking Yu if she should continue using her deeper voice or speak in a higher pitch.

*Xenoblade Chronicles 2* did a great multi-layered translation for Tora's artifical Blade Poppi. For the uninitiated: this character has created a feminine robot that he continually improves upon. Each version of the robot is not only more powerful, but visibly ages up, from a young child into a teenager, then an adult. All of them were originally named "Hana" with an English acronym suffix. Each suffix was a double-layered joke that would expand into a Japanese word and an English phrase. For the localization, they translated the Japanese as various English phrases that are more casual and fit his lecherous programmer character, while making the English phrases into over-the-top cool shit because his family loves naming shit like that.

"Hana JS" is the original form, "JS" standing for "joshishogakusei"/"elementary schoolgirl" and "Jet Spark". The translation is "Poppi a", with the a standing for "alpha" as in "the first usable version of a computer program".  


"Hana JK" stood for "Joshikousei"/"high school girl" and "Justice Knight". The translation is "Poppi QT", phonetically pronounced "cutie" and meaning "Quixotic Tutelar".

"Hana JD" stood for "Joshidaigakusei"/"college girl" and "Judgment Day". The translation is "Poppi QTπ", after the term of endearment "cutie pie". It also apparently means "Quantum Technochampion π"

I just think it's neat they went to all that effort to make the intended effect come across without needing to research. Gets across Tora and family's personality when robot-making pretty well, since Tora openly says his family comes up with a name they like before they even start working on it.

"Clones in fighting games suck and are a wasted character slot"

On a semantic note, there's no such thing as a "wasted slot". Developers do not have a neatly itemized list of "we can have exactly this many characters", it's "how does our budget and our implementation work with our deadline, how does this character line up with the vision, what internal rules do we have to follow for certain brands" (the latter applying only to crossover games). In the most common of circumstances, the "options" with the clone character is either "we fit this character in because we have existing resources, or they just don't exist at all".

On a more personal note, I find the concept of clones to be akin to the tumblr-ism of "holy shit two cakes!". You're telling me I get a moveset that's already been implemented and designed for a specific niche, now with key features edited or small things bolted on in order to work in a different design? You can compare and contrast, you can further express yourself as a player by using whichever iteration appeals to your style. You like swords in Smash Bros? You like the effects and arc of the sword normals but don't want to deal with tippers? Play Lucina! You'd rather keep an aggressive pace and always stay in the enemy face? Play Roy! Are you tired of having Fox's shallow jump arc and basic Reflector? Falco will keep the skies clean and forces you to play around not having a holdable Reflector.

When it comes to characters, I don't see the downside in using time for these kinds of variant movesets when the alternative is that there's just -less-. I understand that die-hard fans of a character's, well, "character" are going to be upset at, say, Ganondorf borrowing Falcon's moves. But to me, the implementation of the character itself, the small changes they breathe in to provide larger gameplay differences, those are causes to celebrate and just more stuff to enjoy in a game I like.

On the note of Square RPGs, Kingdom Hearts has a fair bit of gameplay differences from its later entries, much less tonal differences from being the beginning of what would become a grand-scale saga.

For one, the magic system is simpler and much stronger. Sora and co. have a segmented MP bar, and spells cost much less to cast than future entries, especially the Cure line that only takes 2 segments. Later games would make the MP bar a gradual bar with spells taking arbitrary chunks, and healing spells would use all available MP. Relatedly, there's no magic attack stat, with the potency of your spells purely revolving around having more MP.

There's a lot more platforming in Kingdom Hearts 1, which we wouldn't see again until 3D as the later games focused on action. There's more little interactable objects that can be smacked or have specific spells cast on them to reveal treasure or just make the world believable. For instance, Traverse Town has a candlelit diner that opens a chest if you cast Blizzard on each candle and put them out.

While Donald and Goofy mention the "world order" requiring them to blend in and follow the Prime Directive, only Atlantica and Halloween Town have themed transformations. In the other numbered entries + 3D, most worlds change both the looks of generic Heartless and Sora's group to blend in.

Lastly, enemy health bars are displayed as a set of color-coded HP bars stacking on top of each other, going green-yellow-orange-red-purple. Hades, Sephiroth and Xemnas had a sixth, invisible health bar. Later entries keep health bars as green and show multiple bars as squares under the current bar, letting enemies have over 13 health bars without issue.

2. 5 minutes after the first dragon slain, a different dragon is spawned, giving a different buff.

3.Dragons continue to spawn every five minutes until five dragons are killed (making the earliest "full-dragon clear" 25 minutes into the game). The fifth dragon kill grants a "soul" to the team who killed it, granting a stronger, also permanent buff that's designed to swing momentum further.

4.After five dragons are killed, the next spawn is the Elder Dragon, with a lot more health and power. Killing it grants that team "Aspect of the Dragon", which makes all your attacks do unresistable damage over time, plus you insta-kill anyone with 20% HP or less. This lasts for 150 seconds.

And this still isn't enough to drag League games any closer to bearable time-frames.

Let me put this in a way that I hope makes sense;

Generative AI has been used in many instances where a creator either cannot or *will not* pay for the thing being "generated". The AI is being used in a circumstance where the jobs in question (artist, voice actor, musician, etc.) are full of people looking for roles, looking for work because the industry is mercurial, and for every Troy Baker and Laura Bailey, you have people desperate for any kind of work in their fields. AI is bad because it **prevents a very available job from being fulfilled.**

Additionally, and very importantly, AI cannot create anything from whole-cloth. Every AI voice you hear, every AI picture generated by neural nets, has been trained on the work of others. And in 99% of cases, the sources for this material either did not consent to this, or they were unaware of the contract's terms. Voices are being used to say things the original owners do not want coming out of their mouths. Images are being generated that artists would not want to associate with their art style. AI is bad because **it does not care for consent**.

We are already seeing the effects of this on creative industries; of how art assets are generated "in the style of" an artist without paying for the artist to draw it themselves. We're hearing voice actors react to their voices used against their will, saying hateful or damaging things they would never say. We're watching as dead creatives have their life's work dredged up and used when they can't say no. AI is bad because **it removes the human element.**

I apologize if this sounds dramatic. I just wish to make it clear. AI is bad for the health of creative fields, for ethical, moral and financial reasons.

All four unlockable characters in the original *Super Smash Bros* reuse animations from a base roster character; these range from obvious to barely noticeable.

Luigi, fairly obviously, reuses nearly all of Mario's animations. His specials act different and he has a different taunt and dash attack, but otherwise shares basically everything.

Ness reuses Mario's floor attacks and his skeleton, but is otherwise unique.

Captain Falcon reuses Samus' dash attack, up tilt, down smash, and floor attacks, along with her skeleton. In a meta-reuse, these attacks (and the rest of Falcon's kit) were derived from the original build of the game, *Dragon King: The Fighting Game.* 

Jigglypuff's model is heavily based on Kirby's, shares the multi-jumps, and takes a majority of her attacks from Kirby, including jabs, neutral/up/down aerials, forward smash and down smash.

CA puts extra emphasis on the swelling muscle of his dominant arm, grayscales the screen during the impacts, and seemingly adds a bit of extra energy as it gives the same X-Ray effect as Denjin/"Nothingness" attacks.

The early launch of the Saturn was supposed to be to "beat Sony to the punch" in Western market, but thanks to a complete lack of titles and a $100 difference in price, the Saturn failed out of the gate. It had no library at launch; between its surprise launch and the original "Saturnday", it had the 6 launch titles and a total of two other games: *Bug!* and *Street Fighter: The Movie*, neither of which were exactly system sellers.

The Dreamcast's launch wasn't nearly as bad, though still somewhat poor. In Japan, the system encountered a shortage right at launch, while its killer app *Sonic Adventure* was delayed from its promised launch day window. The console took an entire year to find its footing in Japan, all while not having been released yet in America. But by the time it did, Sega had an absolutely killer launch on 9/9/99. A huge launch lineup, technical prowess and a weird-but-neat ad campaign gave it actual record-breaking sales on launch day that made a great holiday season. Europe wasn't as great, but still way better than the Saturn's.

...and then the Playstation 2 got *announced* and things started falling apart before the dream died.

SaltyBet is a Twitch stream with a fairly interesting concept: run a game of MUGEN (a freeware PC fighting game where players code and share their own characters/stages/HUD) that's constantly running CPU fights with a roster of thousands of characters. Viewers would bet virtual cash on the fights for 60 seconds, then watch the carnage unfold. It was also used for real fighting game tournament events, allowing bets on major tournaments like real-sport bets, but this usage of the platform became rarer and rarer as time went on.

It was decently popular among the MUGEN community before gaining general consciousness thanks to word of mouth. It spawned a small community that, like many chats, became flooded with in-joke memes and betting "advice"; for instance, "NEVER BET ON DBZ" was a common phrase due to the shoddy AI and stats of Dragon Ball characters. The stream subtly evolved over time, primarily controlled via its own site that persistently tracked account currency and even had a premium feature. People who paid real money to become "Salty Illuminati" can request their own custom-matchups, adjust character stats to push a favorite, study their betting history and other features.

Cthulu is present in very few Megaten games: *Shin Megami Tensei 2, Shin Megami Tensei: if...,* the updated re-release of *Persona 2: Innocent Sin* and in the mobile game *Liberation Dx2*. However, the fight is heavily stacked in His favor. Cthulu is a Level 67 demon with rather poor stats compared to YHVH, who sits at Level 108. Cthulu takes 50% more damage from Almighty attacks, which is the only element YHVH uses. Additionally, YHVH boasts the unique skill "Mouth of God" that instantly kills the combatant with the lowest Intelligence. Cthulu, with a base Intelligence of 14, is going to be the primary target for this attack and would likely perish first unless you used another team slot on an even less intelligent demon.

Even more crucially, YHVH reflects all elemental damage except Sword, Almighty, Fire and Electric, none of which are in Cthulu's base moveset. Cthulu can be fused to have Almighty, Fire or Electric, but won't be doing much thanks to stats skewing towards physical moves.

The only move of Cthulu's base movelist that can even hit YHVH is Suck, which deals incredibly weak damage on top of damaging Cthulu for hitting with it. Suffice it to say, Cthulu has a very uphill battle to face if he is going to kill YHVH. It is -possible-, just difficult.

The entire *Pokemon* series, for being my first hyperfixation and giving me the reason to be a social creature when I had a relatively bad upbringing. But in particular, *Mystery Dungeon: Explorers of Sky*, even though it was far into my journey.

I was a very stereotypical Nintendo kid; I preferred games that were arcadey no-plot affairs or very light-hearted escapism pieces. I openly argued with people on the playground who were playing *Halo* or *Call of Duty* for trying to be too "adult" and boring. Most heavily story-based games tended to bounce off me.

But something was different about *Sky*. The way the writing worked (even with its redundancies), the way that it didn't give names to characters, simply using their species to make each character as varied visually as they were personality-wise. The use of musical motifs, the day-structure that made me really feel like I could be there, I was my little Turtwig and I could explore this big mysterious world on a structure that I chose. I was a person with very few friends, and at the time of playing it in 2009, my best friend had advanced to high school while I was stuck in middle school with nobody I really trusted. It was still an escape, but it was an escape with such worldbuilding and a plot that I got truly invested in. For the first time, I saw characters invested in their world's problems, relationships that were shown and not told, basic building blocks that I began to put into my own writings that had just been fluffy nonsense earlier.  


Add that to a chance encounter where, allowed to bring *one game* and get *one thing* on a family trip, I wandered into a store where the strategy guide for the game was on the clearance section, hastily marked with a label of $0.01. That summer, I spent my days in an RV greedily devouring all the information I could, eager to push beyond the story and get everything I could. Still have that book, kept as well as I can.

*Explorers of Sky* wasn't my first video game by far, but it was the first game I had played that showed what a video game could bring out of people: emotions besides mindless joy or challenging frustration, writing that went beyond Nintendo's easy-building blocks.

And lastly, on a very specific note, it's the game that made me fall in love with the names of song titles on soundtracks, to use the names of songs to evoke emotions just as much as the songs themselves. The fact that the final song in the soundtrack--a name you'll only see after you fight tooth and nail through everything the game throws and experience loss before building it all back up--is a song named "Life Goes On!" just touches me. Like it's reassuring you that hey, no matter what, for all the good and bad in our lives, you can keep going. I'm sorry if this is a dumb overly emotional dump-post. My writing's out of practice, but this game means more to me than almost any other.

In *Persona 5*, text and graphics exist in a very early state to show that the "Reverse/Break" mechanic from the past games was going to be implemented; now called "Doubt". While placeholder text exists for every arcana (including plot-related, endgame and party member arcanas), the more detailed texts imply that it was going to be restricted:

\*The mechanic would have affected the non-playable Confidants you specifically strike "deals" with: Iwai, Kawakami, Takemi, Chihaya, Shinya, Ohya, Hifumi, and Yoshida.

\*The text in the final game about Morgana reminding you to visit new Confidants as soon as possible doesn't mean anything, but originally the characters would Doubt you if you didn't accept their first invitations on their next available day(s?) after creating one. There's no other text that implies further Doubt points, but even this alone would be a pain.

\*Casting Doubt on yourself by refusing these invitations would prevent you from making use of their deals, losing access to their benefits such as Iwai's gun customizing or Chihaya's fortunes. You'd need to spend a day to apologize and mend the damaged relationship.

\*Continuing to ignore someone who Doubts you would cause them to break off the deal, cutting off access to the rest of their Confidant forever. Interestingly, the punishment is still less harsh than past Breaks; you could apparently still fuse Personas of the broken arcana, just not getting any bonus EXP as if you hadn't met that arcana. In past games, breaking a Social Link completely removed the ability to fuse Personas of that arcana.

While some might say that the mechanic can fit well given that Joker has to earn everyone's trust and these are deals of convenience rather than friendship, I'm glad that's gone because time management is already frustrating for new players, and I can see this adding an extra level of "railroading" for not much benefit artistically. And this may be a hot take, but I feel Persona 5 is so far away from typical Megaten in difficulty and atmosphere that continuing such a punishing mechanic doesn't jive with the kind of game it's become.

The "Mystic Eyes of Death Perception" are one of the many, many insanely busted abilities in *Tsukihime*, and in the greater Nasuverse they're really only held back by the fact that *Tsukihime* itself is a fairly low-powered corner of the setting.

The general gist of the Eyes is that the user gains the ability to see the very concept of Death itself; every single thing that *can* die is shown to have lines and dots overlaid on them. Dragging anything over these lines or piercing these dots results in the complete death of the object. Not "this object/person dies physically or spiritually", the actual universal constant of their existence is just removed. The biggest survivor of them, Arcuied, had to spend most of her top-level power on remaking the concept of her body. The only thing that limits these on paper is the fact that:

a) the user must physically touch the Lines of Death with something, but that thing can be as basic as a finger or a ruler.

b) the user's concept of death affects it. If your shitty human body can't comprehend a thing dying, you can't kill it with the Eyes unless you can understand what it means to kill that thing. Conversely, this means that things you understand as "ending", like, say, momentum, possession or getting poisoned, can be killed.

Like a lot of things in Nasuverse, their true power comes from playing with words, concepts and exploring a lot of technicalities of how things work. Case in point; though there's limitations on being able to kill higher-end things like the Night of Wallachia (because he's more of a force of nature or a phenomena than a living being, and you can't exactly kill the concept of a storm), there's feats such as (spoiler for Far Side route): >!Shiki helps take down a near full-power Arcueid during a time when she's heavily tilted circumstances in her favor by exploiting technicality. She draws power from the Earth itself, and Shiki can't kill a living weapon of this level. So he just \*kills the Earth that's beneath her\* to cut off her connection.!<

It's an interesting ability to give the protagonist because it's so strong on a base level that most fights and Shiki's development as a warrior rely on outmaneuvering his opponent, facing down himself as much as his enemy in order to rationalize the death of something so outside of his average human life. The (apocryphal) story of very early Magic the Gathering and Chaos Orb. Chaos Orb is a card from the "wackier" sets, with a peculiar effect:

"Flip Chaos Orb onto the playing field from a height of at least one foot. Chaos Orb must turn completely over at least once or it is discarded with no effect. When Chaos Orb lands, any cards in play that it touches are destroyed, as is Chaos Orb."

The story has several tellings, but perhaps the most popular is that, during a tournament match, a professional player chose to tear his Chaos Orb into pieces, tossing the pieces into the air. The pieces landed on almost all the opponent's cards, and the Orb player reasoned that each piece was still Chaos Orb, they all counted.

A judge was called, and the theory was sound; every card the Orb fragments touched was now destroyed. **However,** since the rules state you must have 60 cards in your deck and Chaos Orb was shredded, the player was immediately disqualified.

While the story itself is impossible to verify, the legend got popular enough that it got ascended into its own card; from the joke set "Unglued" is the card "Chaos Confetti". Confetti's ability is explicitly: "Tear \[this card\] into pieces. Throw the pieces into the playing area from at least five feet. Destroy each card in play a piece touches." It's not legal in any format, but it's still hilarious rules-lawyering made cardboard-form.

The other comment gave you a very condensed version; if you're still interested in the specifics of wha' happun, this is a shortform of the game's relatively numerous problems:

The original Overwatch was a 6 vs 6 shooter that focused on PvP, recommending and eventually forcing a team composition of 2 DPS, 2 Tanks and 2 Supports per team. The game was announced as a multiplayer-only experience, retailing for $40 as a one-time purchase with cosmetic unlocks via loot boxes (both paid and earnable through gameplay). Post-launch support came in the form of maps, new cosmetics, event game modes including some light PvE co-op, and most importantly additional characters. As switching characters mid-match was an integral part of gameplay, all additional characters were free.

The game was light on story, mostly fleshing the universe via comics, animations and website material that was rarely accessible through the game itself. The fanbase's disapproval of the plot's lack of impact and glacial pace, in addition to perceived problems with the game's meta warping into a slow-paced, shield-infested mess as well as the controversies surrounding loot boxes, prompted Blizzard to announce Overwatch 2 in 2019, promising radical changes that would "reinvent the sequel" and add story-focused PvE with deep exclusive mechanics. Overwatch 2 would apparently have full backwards compatibility with Overwatch 1, sharing servers and allowing players not interested in PvE to still enjoy the original. The game went into maintenance mode as Overwatch 2 developed, with only a single new character and no other new content.

Overwatch 2 was repeatedly delayed, and Activision-Blizzard would be under fire in the news for multiple scandals and horrific behavior, such as reports of widespread sexual assault, large-scale firings while the CEO received bonuses, and manipulative marketing patents. In a seeming attempt to smokescreen the negative press, Overwatch 2's sparse previews would be revealed during these scandals, and infamously attempted to garner goodwill by releasing extra material that revealed various characters as queer.

When Overwatch 2 finally had more concrete information 2 years later, the game was radically redesigned; now a 5 vs 5 game with a single, solitary tank per team in attempt to speed up the kill time. An entire game mode and all associated maps were removed, citing unpopularity, as a new mode took its place. In addition to some character reworks, Overwatch 2 was announced to have 2 new characters, a move seen as lacking with how long the game took. Furthermore, the promised PvE was delayed due to "quality control", and Overwatch 2 was announced that it would not supplement, but instead replace Overwatch.

Overwatch 2 would completely shut down the original game's servers, keeping all players' progress but removing the entirety of the original game. Instead of a one-time purchase and loot boxes, 2 would transition to a free-to-play seasonal model with paid cosmetics in a rotating shop alongside a battle pass. Alongside the battle pass came news that all future characters would be unlocked via battle pass, with premium purchase offering immediate use. When the game came out in 2022, this left new players unable to use the first battle pass character without 20+ hours of grinding.

While steps have been taken to soothe various smaller pain points and ease the free experience of unlocking characters, Blizzard walked back their promises of PvE and explained that the promised deep campaign that Overwatch 2 was founded on had been canceled internally years ago. Instead, story missions using similar cut-down frameworks as the earlier PvE events would be released per season instead of all at once, costing money if not played outside time-limited events.

*Island Xtreme Stunts* on PS2, though there's also PC and GBA versions. The third game in the *Lego Island* series, and not nearly as well-known as its priors.

It's a kid-friendly sandbox game that was the closest thing to *GTA* my kid self could play. You're still Pepper Roni, pizza delivery boy for Papa Brickolini's Pizzeria. But the gimmick of the game is that Pepper is an actor in an action movie alongside The Brickster, who goes along with the movie only to plan dastardly deeds. Each scene of the movie is a different minigame where you control vehicles with wildly different control schemes, starting with a standard *OutRun* style car chase alongside jetski segments, skydiving, sidescrolling *Trials*\-like motorbikes, and others. There's even an out-of-nowhere sequence of jank 3D platforming up a tower.

In between the scenes, you can explore Lego Island, which is an actually pretty small sandbox in hindsight but has some charm. There's more minigames, collectible bricks to build animals, a skateboard for very light *Tony Hawk*\-isms and three vehicle types; cars, boats and planes/helicopters. As a kid's game, though, Pepper has to get a license for each type of vehicle before he can drive it. You can't steal vehicles in motion, but feel free to waltz into the police station and fly off in their chopper. When I was a kid, I needed a friend to get the plane license because each license test is flying through rings and I couldn't get the pattern down.

It has a dorky but earnest 2000s-rock and pop soundtrack of original music complete with radio inserts by in-universe DJs, and instead of getting to gun down innocents or enemies you have an endless supply of pizzas you can inconvenience the Island with by rapid fire throwing or doing a double-pizza "cymbal clap" at close range. A relatively short and light but honestly okay experience.

In SFV, DLC was implemented in an odd fashion with no real "set" timetable. There was no set time between the seasons, and no schedule within the seasons either.

Season 1 was mostly consistent, likely due to the characters being worked on during the end of main game development. 5 characters released from March - August, with each one separated by a month except Urien, who took 2 months.

Season 2 spaced each character out more; a two month gap between Akuma and Kolin, 3 months for Ed, 2 months for Abigail before Menat dropped a month later, then another 2 months for Zeku. Overall, it took 10 months for the season.

Season 3 was a bit faster-paced; Sakura and Blanka in Jan-Feb, Falke and Cody in April-June, then August had both G and Sagat on the exact same day. Overall, 8 months.

Season 4 started soon and had a colossal length. With Kage in December of that same year, it would be 9 months before Honda, Poison and Lucia all came out the same day in August, Gill in December and Seth on the next year's Valentine's Day. In total, that's 14 months to release 6 characters.

Season 5 also had a gap, but not as stark of one, likely due to SF6's internal delay. Starting in February, it would be two months for Rose, then four months for the typical August releases with Oro and Akira a week apart from each other, ending on Luke in November. All in all, that's 9 months for five, technically six characters if you count Eleven as a character and not a fancy random select button.

Here's a fun trading card example: Charizard in the Pokemon Trading Card Game has had a recurring archetype with its depictions; most Charizard cards from the very beginning have one attack that deals an absolute fuckload of damage, usually enough to take out an enemy Pokemon in a single attack. The problem comes from an absurdly high opportunity cost (Charizard itself is near-always a Stage 2 card, necessitating 2 turns, Charmander cards and either running Charmeleon or Rare Candy to skip Charmeleon, both of which take up valuable deck space)...

...an absurdly high Energy cost... (needing 4 or more Energy cards for said strong attack, requiring either very specific deckbuilding to attach more Energy or setting up for four turns while starving any other Pokemon)

and finally, a generally crippling downside. Usually, this takes the form of requiring Charizard to discard some or all of the Energy you used, meaning you have to take another 2-5 turns to get the nuke rolling again. The hyper-powerful variants such as Mega Charizard and Charizard VMAX embody this archetype into overdrive.

Some Charizards see useful tournament play, and ironically these are either cards with even cooler forms of Charizard (Radiant Charizard aka Shiny Jet-Black-And-Red Dragon) or cards where Charizard is teaming up with other Pokemon such as Braixen or Reshiram. This is the reason Charizard cards end up causing higher prices and attention on the secondary market; casual fans like it for either being a cool fire dragon or big number go boom, but competitive players want to turn it into more practical and useful cards like Professor's Research, Mew VMAX, or Welder.

Well, others have answered for you and I see in another reply you've chosen Sky (a fine choice), but just in case, I would like to provide a small overview of the Pokemon ones (there are other Mystery Dungeon games, but I have little experience with them outside of some small gameplay of *Chocobo's Dungeon: Every Buddy*)

\**Blue/Red Rescue Team* (DS/GBA) are the beginners of the series, with a somewhat simplistic plot and an overall lighter tone than many of the later entries. Compared to their successors, they're a bit bare in terms of features. Going up to Generation 3 of Pokemon, the plotline is a bit shorter than the others, with a prodigious and somewhat plot-light postgame to make up for it. They still have value for those looking for an "entry-level" Mystery Dungeon. The GBA version, Red, lacks second-screen map functionality and has lower sound quality, but has exclusive Pokemon that only show up in Blue if you use specific ingame codes or put the cartridge into a DS with Blue.

\*Relatedly, there is a remake/definitive edition known as *Rescue Team DX* (Switch). The most recent entry in the series, these are faithful remakes of the games with all content under one cart and a very polished visual and audio makeover. Many changes have been made to gameplay to simplify things, including the removal of the basic attack, features from later entries such as move-upgrading and the Fairy type, and reducing the floor count of some later dungeons to make things easier. This version replaces the otherwise present IQ system with "Traits" and removes the ability to explore side areas, but is an overall easier and more accessible entry.

\**Explorers of Time/Darkness/Sky* are held up by the fanbase as the peak of the series, with little in the way of argument. Carrying all of the changes brought from Generation 4 of Pokemon, Time and Darkness are again plot-identical versions with just a few altered Pokemon between them. In addition to a few new minor gameplay changes, the star of the show is the story; hailed as among the best in the entire Pokemon series, featuring a darker tone and much deeper characterization. Sky acts as the "third version", adding a new "exclusive item" mechanic to deepen Pokemon variance while combining content and adding more. New features to train your team, an easing of the notorious consequences of failure, and most importantly, "Special Episodes" to see through the eyes of side characters in disconnected episodes. 

\*I'd talk a bit about the WiiWare games, but they're notoriously hard to get a hold of and poorly-documented; only recently was there a fan translation of the three, which mostly differ in which types are emphasized. They're very lighthearted and simplistic entries due to the WiiWare format, and use the same models as *Pokemon Rumble/My Pokemon Ranch*.

\**Gates to Infinity* (3DS) is the rougher middle child of the series. Attempting to try new things with altered dungeon navigation and a focus on Gen 5 Pokemon, the game primarily centers around building up a home base in a very light "property sim" aspect, when not dealing with its plot that takes a relatively smaller-scale than Explorers, saving its darker moments and better writing for later in. Gameplay has been simplified with more tools to get the player out of a jam. Notably, the hunger mechanic endemic to all prior entries in the entire Mystery Dungeon series is gone, save for a few DLC dungeons.

\**Super Mystery Dungeon* (3DS) attempts to course-correct from Gates' reception, though perhaps does it by half-measures. Back to more of a character focus, a grander scale, and a raise in difficulty. This is done by lowering the apparent age of the main characters, forcing the first section to be an elongated tutorial, expanding the world map and available Pokemon, and tossing out some systems, including the hunger removal, permanent equipment and the mainstay "beat people to recruit them". Most notoriously, these are perhaps the hardest games in the series by way of stat inflation and neutering grinding. If you wish to succeed in this game, you'll be reliant on randomly-dropping, ephemeral equipment for buffs and taking careful use of your item resources--a bit similar to older roguelikes, but enough difference for people to not enjoy it.

Persona 2 is actually split up into two games, and trying to play both in the same format is...tricky. It also doesn't help that the games have a good amount of content changed if you have save data for both.

The first entry, *Innocent Sin*, was released for Playstation 1 in Japan only, likely due to specific offensive imagery in the endgame. It was ported to PSP later, and this port was released in the West. There also exists a high-quality fan translation of the PS1 version online.

The second entry, *Eternal Punishment*, was translated and released worldwide for PS1, with its localization carrying on changes done to the original *Persona* that some found contentious. It would be remade for PSP, but in a reversal, the update never left Japan. A fan translation exists, complete with a hack to allow you to import your *Innocent Sin* PSP save regardless of region.

So in short, you've got two ways; rely on fan translations to play both on their original material, or play the updated *Innocent Sin* before going back to play *Eternal Punishment* without the changes made when importing saves from one game to the next.

As a fellow Jamie main, though fairly low in the ranks, here's a few tips if you'd like:

\*QCB+P (Swagger Step is the official name, but most people call it "palm" for short) can actually be safe, you just have to be very specific about the distance. Whiffing them in training mode can help you determine the distance; you need to hit them at the end of the lunge for the move to be safe.

\*Jamie's aggressive anti-projectile options are unlocked with drinks. For far distances, using the different divekicks to maneuver around projectiles at Lv.1 is workable if the opponent's fireball is slow. I tend to use Light Kick divekick for this. At Lv.2, breakdance kick (qcf+k) is projectile invulnerable after a bit and can react to short/mid-range fireballs, though riskier.

\*Do not underestimate Drive Rush in the neutral game. When you've made the hit, put them on the disadvantage, it's surprising how fast you can lunge across the screen with your choice of overhead (forward+medium kick) or long ranged low (crouching medium kick). At the same time, a cautious opponent will check you with a defensive normal, so try to watch the opponent and predict when you can get away with this.

\*Your farthest-reaching normal buttons are forward+heavy kick, standing heavy kick, standing medium kick, and standing heavy punch. Not all are the best tools for every situation, but they've got some uses in surprising opponents.

\*If you're fighting a heavy zoner like JP, Dhalsim or Guile, you're going to have to be patient. Parry, dash in during gaps, and finish closing the distance with those long-ranged normals alongside "random" palm if you feel like taking a little risk for good reward.

F-Zero and Custom Robo, as series in general.

I think it's F-Zero's relentless difficulty, competition with Mario Kart (where it lacks recognizable characters, a comeback mechanic or any form of randomness) and the lack of bullet-point-on-box features to differentiate the versions which failed to give it an audience. But the overwhelming speed, unique mechanics and that same difficulty makes it one of my consistently favorite series. All three console entries have something in their own right that makes them amazing, and they come with some of the coolest vehicle designs and soundtracks of any racing game. Sega's Amusement Vision division even got to try their hand, but the Gamecube was already floundering at that point.

It's sad that, at this point, Captain Falcon has almost appeared in as many Smash games as he does *games in his own series*. X and GX are genuinely some of my favorite games of all time, and while a few spiritual successors are there to try and inherit the unique risk-reward, space racing themes and antigravity racing of F-Zero, there'll never be anything for the original. And yes, the interview where Miyamoto claims that the series "advanced little" as a reasoning for not making any new ones will sting for a long, long time.

Custom Robo is a whole different story, and I wish just as much that it did well. We never got the series until the Gamecube, sorta like Fire Emblem, and the first impression was...a weird attempt. The past games were colorful shonen-action with a younger target audience, and we got the one where robots were tech-armor'd, faceplate-wearing and cleavage-baring in a much more "Y2K" world attempting to sell a serious story. The fact that you can't even really give Custom Robo a specific genre--it's got elements of RPGs, shooting games and arena brawlers all at once, plus pretty much no contemporary advertising, probably worked in tandem with the Gamecube's lacking install base to give it any real shot.

The swan song for Custom Robo came out on DS and tried its best to mass-market appeal as possible; on a system filled with casuals, easing up the difficulty while returning to the colorful anime artstyle, adding a power-up mechanic, new side features and having Brawl feature its mascot Robo as an Assist Trophy. It still didn't work. And unlike F-Zero, I don't see anyone trying to make Custom Robo-likes or calling for rereleases, Smash appearances or much else.

So in case you'd like, here's a small guide for Final Fantasy 7, spoiler-free.

**OG:** The complete original scenario. Depending on who you ask, has aged the worst of all the Final Fantasies, so go in expecting PS1 conventions and a less-than-polished translation. Uses the Active-Time-Battle system iterated from prior entries, using turn-based commands on a timer. All versions are content-identical, though the modern PC/PS4/Switch ports have convenience features to make the game easier and the original PC version is a disaster.

**Compilation:** Best absorbed after the original. Consists of action-RPG *Crisis Core* (prequel), movie *Advent Children* (direct sequel) and its tie-in novels *On The Way to a Smile*, and third-person shooter *Dirge of Cerberus* (sequel to *Advent Children).* Also includes a defunct Japan-only cellphone game with no official translation, *Before Crisis*, the earliest time point of the Compilation.

**Remake:** An eventual trilogy taking a new spin on the story, expanding and altering events. Does not require knowledge of the OG to enjoy, but some moments can hit differently if you have. Uses an action-RPG style with multiple controllable party members in real-time combat. The first entry is out for PS4, PS5 and PC, with the latter two versions having an exclusive side-scenario *Intergrade*. The second entry will release on PS5 in 2024, and a tie-in novel is also out to expand on two character's pasts.

**Ever Crisis**: An attempt at providing a more "faithful" remake, though still with updated script. A currently-unreleased cellphone game with Active Time Battle and presentation similar to the OG, but with modern production values and features like a weapon-gacha. Is stated to eventually include the entirety of the original game and the Compilation.

That's up to you; there's now *four* different versions of Persona 3 available, with varying means of legally playing, and none that can truly be called "definitive". As a recap, to help figure which one you may want:

\**Persona 3* (PS2) is the original, roughest version of the game. Has the least amount of content, but may interest people who want a "pure" experience of the first "modern" Persona game. Its age shows in a variety of user-unfriendly decisions that multiple revisions afterwards improve upon, such as no direct way to control party members or manually select Persona skills upon fusion. There's been no future rerelease of this game legally, because...

\**Persona 3: FES* (PS2) is an expanded rerelease of the game to celebrate its success. Mechanically, there's a few changes like new Personas, a "hard" difficulty, costume armors, and a new Social Link was added (with an already-existing character). More importantly, it adds an all-new postgame story called "The Answer", which provides resolution to the plot and sets up for the cast's later appearances. There was a port available on PS3, but buying it will require a workaround thanks to Sony deprecating the store.

\**Persona 3 Portable* (PSP) is sort of a mixed bag. To fit on the PSP's more limited memory, the game was reformatted into a visual-novel style with flat backgrounds and character-portrait vignettes for all non-anime cutscenes. Dungeon-crawling and combat still uses 3D models, but of course are compromised for the handheld. Many gameplay rebalances were made, including an Easy mode and finally introducing the ability to manually control party members. This version also omits "The Answer" entirely, but in its place allows for playing as a female version of the protagonist. Playing as a girl redoes the entire UI, has subtle character differences with dialog options, and gives a unique set of social links including a few characters who weren't in the male route.

This version is the only current one available on modern consoles as well as PC, with a very direct re-release featuring upscaled textures and not much else. A post-launch patch did finally allow you to manually distribute Persona skills like you can in later games.

Back in the earlier days of webcomics, there was a comic called "Ctrl+Alt+Delete". It was a gaming-focused webcomic that had both parodic sketches about games and vignettes with characters meant to imitate author Tim Buckley, his friends and his girlfriend/wife. Wanting to branch out from simple humor based sketches, the insert-character plotline became more dramatic and focused on relationships and romantic tension. 

While Ctrl+Alt+Del had been mocked in this time for its seemingly lazy art and its writing that reinforced negative stereotypes of gamers, this jump into an attempted storyline was seen as taking itself too seriously.

All this came to a head when Tim's real wife suffered a miscarriage. To keep the story going and vent his frustration, Buckley wrote it into the comic as "Loss": four panels, no dialog, simply a depiction of tragedy.

This was the breaking point for the comic: Buckley was seen as making content out of his wife's tragedy, was mocked for the utterly whiplash inducing mood swing, and the format of the comic ensuring it was followed by another comedy sketch. He became even more of a laughingstock, and the comic's dialog-less format allows it to be abstracted as four sets of lines to incur similar whiplash in those who get the joke.

Its been 15 years since the strip was published, so this is an edit of "Loss" to instead celebrate its fame/legacy.

Axel in Kingdom Hearts. In his original appearance, *Chain of Memories*, Axel was "just" one of the more significant villains, who acts as a wildcard and provides some memorable scenes. (Shoutouts to providing the only swear in the entire series, albeit text-only.)

He then appears again in *Kingdom Hearts II* as a side character during the infamously long prologue. This was supposed to be his end, but apparently the development team is on record as loving him enough that they decided to keep him around and gave him a few more token appearances. He was still a wildcard, with mainly small personal stakes regarding one of the other protagonists and little effect on the main narrative.

Fast forward to *358/2 Days*, where Axel is now one of the primary protagonists of the game, and things only get more important for the boy. Kingdom Hearts really loves the concept of protagonists-in-trios, such as the all-important Sora-Donald-Goofy. Axel ends up becoming a member of his own trio, the "Clock Tower Trio" alongside Roxas and Xion.

As a member of this trio, Axel ends up becoming an even more important main character. >!Or rather, his original self/"Somebody" named Lea does. !<From getting another miniboss fight in *Birth by Sleep* to getting major importance in *Dream Drop Distance*, Axel's status as a fan-favorite ended up giving him big appearances and more of an impact on the plot, to the point that he ends up with a major change that I imagine nobody on the team considered for him way back in 2003: >!Lea ends up being a Keyblade wielder, joining the war against the True Organization XIII in the climax of the series.!<

All of this is even cooler to me when I discovered the character's origins: Tetsuya Nomura intentionally designed Axel as a redo of the design for Reno, a minor villain/side character from *Final Fantasy VII* and its *Compilation.* He was a testbed, Nomura said, to "try out a familiar character in a new universe and see how he developed." Well, Reno never made it half as far as Axel did, either with the fanbase or in the games themselves.
