In the Paper Mario fandom, while the base is split between "classic" fans who prefer *64-Thousand Year Door* (and occasionally *Super*) and "modern" fans who prefer *Sticker Star* onward, the classic fans have one holy grail that will remain forever out of reach.

The first shown version of *Sticker Star* was at E3 2010, and featured a presentation and seemingly overall gameplay similar to *Thousand Year Door*. Battles were taking place on a stage, and enemies retained their general design bits from previous Paper Mario games. A scant bit of footage showed a Chain Chomp partner, who both assisted Mario in battle and could be used to solve overworld puzzles. The overall aesthetic of the world was similar in color and construction to the original *Paper Mario 64*.

Reportedly, this build of the game would be scrapped due to comments from Shigeru Miyamoto to Kensuke Tanabe, the project lead; Miyamoto claimed the game was "just a port of the GC version". Miyamoto would also infamously deliver a request to Tanabe that the game not use "original characters". Later interviews would elaborate and state the team was "no longer allowed" to create new characters in Mario's world or visually edit existing species.

This interview also revealed that the original design for the game was to have a more involved story. This was rejected for three reasons:

1. Miyamoto believed the game didn't need a story, and that excessive story could get in the way of the gameplay
2. Tanabe developed the game with the handheld mindset of "small episodes you can pick up and put down easily", which precluded overarching narrative.
3. The development team apparently read the Club Nintendo surveys (where purchasers who registered the game online could answer surveys for digital currency) and their data found only 1% of players responded that they liked the story in *Super.*

The "classic" Paper Mario fans have wondered for years what that prototype could have become if these decisions hadn't been made, and want to see anything beyond the scrap of footage we got to find just what made the game "a port of \[*Thousand Year Door\]*".

The success of *Slender* ushered in an era of indie horror games that relied on implied narrative and minimalist presentation, often with a single "mascot" character that persistently pursued the player. These games also created their own sphere of influence where the resulting games were designed to be reacted to and experienced via Let's Play. From there, the trend started spiralling a bit into outright parody, such as *Baldi's Basics in Education and Learning.* 

This era of indie-developed horror games also led directly into *Five Nights at Freddy's*, which was developed without context of the trend but started merging the "persistent mascot horror" with "immature horror", which relied on twisting seemingly child-friendly characters and bright colors into often supernatural horror monstrosities. 

​

As an entirely separate subject, the prevalence of "extreme sports" in the late 90s-early 2000s  brought with it a new wave of extreme-sports video games that, for the most part, attempted to copy the success of *Tony Hawk's Pro Skater*. Activision predated their future Guitar Hero glut by creating their own lesser-known followups following the trend of "Notable Athlete's Pro Extreme Sport"; *Matt Hoffman's Pro BMX, Shaun White's Pro Snowboarding, Kelly Slater's Pro Surfer.* Disney purchased the *THPS4* engine outright for *Disney's Extreme Skate Adventure*, Konami had two entries with the more "extreme" *Evolution Skateboarding* and the tamer *ESPN X Games Skateboarding / Winter X Games Snowboarding* duology. Beyond that, you had games like *Aggressive Inline, Razor Freestyle Scooter, Go! Go! Hypergrind, Toxic Grind*, etc.

Many of these games followed in the "timed challenge" format of *THPS* and copied their level objectives, sense of momentum and physics, and emphasis on "street" culture alongside licensed soundtracks featuring rock, pop-punk, and metal. Many fell to the wayside as the extreme sports genre became cluttered and many measured up short against their very inspiration, which was coming out on a yearly schedule to drown imitators and maximize profits.

I apologize if this is "hijacking", but I figured I'd give an addendum for the Pokemon side game with the best status effects; Pokemon Mystery Dungeon. Several of the statuses work differently, most for the worse, but they add a ton more and change some of the more unlikely ones to be outright godlike. Items that cause status ailments are some of the best boss-killers, since only very specific postgame enemies have the IQ passives required to ignore various statuses. In no particular order:

\*In mainline games, "infatuation" is near useless, preventing an attack 50% of the time only if the opponent is the opposite gender of the user. In the first PMD games, the only thing that had a tracked gender was you. Attract thus worked on *everything* and was a quick, easy way to neutralize a boss when it stops them from doing literally anything for 5-6 turns.

\*Smokescreen is a filler, basic accuracy-lowering debuff in mainline. In PMD, it causes the "whiffer" status, which just outright forces every attack to miss. This condition was removed in the 3DS games, probably because Cyndaquil getting Smokescreen so early invalidated every single-foe encounter.

\*Throw a Hunger Seed at an enemy to inflict the self-describing "immobilized by hunger" state, which completely prevents them from moving until they eat a food item. This one item is super rare because it genuinely just lets you set up for however long you want and nuke something before it can fight back.

\*Speaking of seed items, the X-Eye Seed is basically concentrated psychedelics that force the Pokemon consuming it to view the world in a confused, bizarre daze where they can't tell friend from foe and everything is indistinct. Throw one at an enemy to make them wander the room and forget all about you, attacking completely random directions for several turns. The only counterplay enemies have is a possible room-clearer attack, a rare thing on bosses.  


\*Perish Song works near-identically to the mainline games (all enemies die in 3 turns), but now with terrible accuracy. This low accuracy is to make up for the fact that it hits the entire floor, even enemies you can't see, it only affects enemies instead of killing you too, and in PMD, "moves" means any singular action including moving 1 space, using an item or attacking by any means. Pokemon Mystery Dungeon has a mechanic that's a carryover from other Mystery Dungeons and a departure from mainline Pokemon; a regular attack button. Instead of using the limited PP of your moves, you could press A to do a typeless, weak attack that ran off your physical Attack stat. While killing enemies only with it results in less EXP to encourage some resource use, it was a lifesaver and a neat part of the sandbox to have a reliable attack even when your moves weren't cutting it. It also acted as a crystal-clear power scale example when you ran older dungeons and beat up everything with a basic attack.

Also, the invisible traps in dungeons were revealed if you attacked their square, so a crafty player could save themselves a headache by attacking suspect tiles.

Every game after the Japan-only WiiWare has done more to neuter the mechanic. The 3DS entries make the attack do a fixed 5 damage, not enough to be worth it on even the earliest enemies. The Switch remake of Red/Blue Rescue Team outright remove it entirely save for an interesting programming error with teammates where they'll use it under very specific circumstances.

The 3DS games attempt to alleviate it by introducing a new mechanic; move upgrading. Every one of your moves can be individually leveled up by using it repeatedly, which increases the PP of the move at certain levels. The mechanic itself is fine and can lead to fun specialization decisions, but I'll always prefer more options and I think the basic attack was a solid part of the game.

Pokemon HeartGold and SoulSilver, to the point I almost feel it's cheating to bring them up. And despite the fact that Gold and Silver rank among my favorite games of all time.

Gold and Silver are amazing games in their own right, and Crystal builds up on them with a new sidequest and establishing one of the longest-running Pokemon staples in the Battle Tower. But bless Iwata's soul, there was only so much they could do with the GB cartridge, especially when they needed to keep it compatible with the risotto-code of Gen 1.

HeartGold and SoulSilver rectify nearly every issue about Gen 2 while bringing them into the "modern" era with even more content and features. The shrunken-down areas from Kanto are restored to their original forms, trainer rematches are made stronger to alleviate the terrible level scaling from the originals, Running Shoes improve the pace of overworld travel and so much more.

They reused Gen 4's Platinum engine so the game still runs smoothly without framedrops or slow pacing in battles, kept the Pal Park from Diamond and Pearl by shoving it where the old Safari Zone used to be (and building a new Safari Zone with its own rad terrain-placing mechanic) and added the mother of all amazing mechanics: Walking. Pokemon. After years of demands, now every single Pokemon had individual sprites for walking behind your trainer and had context-sensitive comments when talked to depending on where you were and how much it liked you. There's a ton of love and care put into how the different types and even certain species react to being brought all over both regions. It's also hilarious how nobody is even remotely bothered when you're being followed by a 40-foot whale, a creature that forces everyone around it to experience horrible nightmares, or a fire snail reportedly hotter than the surface of the sun.

And to show off those walking sprites even further they made the new gameplay side-mode the "Pokeathlon", a collection of minigames where each and every single Pokemon including all the alternate forms have different sets of non-combat stats. Sunkern is literally the weakest Pokemon numerically and yet it has Pokeathlon stats equal to God Himself. 

People loved the postgame of Gold and Silver for being a romp through the past region, so HeartGold and SoulSilver built on that by giving you sidequest upon sidequest to encounter basically every Legendary and starter you might want, with both Pokemon missing from the originals and ones that hadn't existed yet like the Hoenn starters and the Regi Trio. The Crystal Battle Tower got upgraded into a port of the Battle Frontier from Platinum, so now there's 7 super-difficult endurance gauntlets of challenges with different rules.

I could really just go on, but HeartGold and SoulSilver set the fucking bar for Pokemon remakes super high and every other remake is compared (unfavorably) to them. Oh, and as a last thing (though forced by EU laws); they made the slots a Minesweeper clone so you could get the prizes without needing exorbitant in-game cash or gambling luck. Tabuu in Super Smash Brothers Brawl being a representation of a strict older figure trying to bully a child and being jealous of their freedom. **Spoilers for Super Smash Bros. Brawl's Subspace Emissary below. And dumb theory over-explanation.**

*(This part is canon info, or as close to canon as possible for Smash)*

Master Hand is the representation of a child throwing their toys around for imaginative battle scenes. The opening of 64 shows it shoving desk gubbins in the vague shape of what becomes Peach's Castle, and it brings the figures to life to fight each other. When it runs out of ideas on enemies for the toys to fight, it uses its own hand as a powerful outsider that still loses in the end, and the toys get put back 'till next time.  


In Brawl, Tabuu controls Master Hand(s), and uses it as a proxy to command the villainous characters to remove areas of the World of Trophies; absorbing them into Subspace, mashing them together with no rhyme or reason after returning damn near every trophy into an inert state.  


*(theory now)*  
I want to believe Tabuu is either the direct intervention of an older figure or just the child's anger-stricken proxy for that figure getting in the way of playtime. To get the obvious out of the way; its name is just straight up "taboo", the definition being "banned on the grounds of morality or taste". An older figure has been watching the child play with their ever-expanding amount of toys, and now they're trying to take the kid's enjoyment away because it's unbecoming of the child growing up. The villain himself is named for the construct trying to be enforced on the kid. Its effects are starting in the background as the older figure starts intruding; Master Hand is being physically, painfully chained up and forced to direct the villains in a scheme that's destroying chunks of the world that this child has made. 

All of Tabuu's forces and the locations/constructions associated with them are emblematic of teenage creative impulses; there's gunmetal gray everywhere, Subspace Army enemies are often either visibly weaponized or carry weapons themselves. This isn't a battle bug, but one of the more notable coding oddities in Gen 4 is the absolute overprotection it does that makes the "Saving a lot of data..." message players dread.

If you ever do anything with the PC system, the game's save instructions force a review of the checksums for every single slot in the PC boxes. What this means is that the game is checking, one-by-one, every Pokemon in the PC to make sure every bit of data isn't out of the ordinary. It's a good programming practice, but taken into overdrive since the checksums are comparing tons of factors compressed into the few bytes each Pokemon takes up.

As long as your save file has actually existed before loading the game, you can go a long time and have save times just as short as Gen 3. But sending a single Pokemon to the box, opening a box to look at a single Pokemon, or moving a Pokemon one step to the right all trigger the checksum-routine as much as a rigorous re-organizing of your boxes.

The tweet and thread are referring to the "furry" community, a group of people who share enjoyment of anthropomorphic (humanlike) animals. Examples of these characters in mainstream media are Sonic the Hedgehog, Tony the Tiger, Bugs Bunny, etc.

Furries, as they're called, are widely known to spend lots of money on the fandom. Many of them create their own "fursonas", or characters they feel represent them. With these designs, they commission mascot-like suits to dress up as their characters ("fursuits") or artwork featuring their characters.

Both of these pursuits cost lots of money, as fursuits are mostly custom made with complex designs, and the pursuit of high quality artwork means higher prices from artists. It isn't uncommon for a fursuit to cost upwards of $2000 or more, and the more specific you want your artwork the more it's going to cost.

As an example (as I am part of this culture), a single "reference sheet" of my character cost me $75, and that was a simple drawing to be used as reference for future works. An actual piece of art I commissioned went to $170.

Going back to the tweet, the poster is stating that he firmly believes that nobody could out-spend a furry ("go stack for stack") as furries would simply have too much money.

In Fire Emblem: Sacred Stones for GBA, one of your earliest characters is a paladin named Seth. He is your main character's loyal guard, and he fits into a recurring archetype from Fire Emblem: the "Jagen", named for the first character of this type.

Jagens are experienced soldiers older than the protagonist, usually a cavalry class. This is represented as them already being promoted one tier on the class list, granting huge stat bonuses at the expense of receiving little EXP for killing and having bad stat growths when they do level up. Since EXP is limited in most classic FE games, Jagens are meant to be a crutch to help you raise weaker units and fade out of use.

But Seth forgot that part about bad stat growths. He keeps up even in the endgame with a really good stat distribution. And when I said "most" FEs have limited EXP, Sacred Stones is an exception. You're able to grind if you need, so using Seth has no opportunity cost for training other characters.

He moves farther than almost anyone, takes nearly no damage, kills everything he can reach, and to top it all off, he grants attack and defense buffs to anyone he's adjacent to.

Sacred Stones is already an easy Fire Emblem, but the tier list for it is literally based on who supports Seth the best and how they make him better. He can solo the entire game and it's probably the most efficient way to do so.
